questions.question: In a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, what does the Chinese postman problem ask for?
options: A closed route that traverses every edge exactly once
A shortest closed route covering every edge at least once
A shortest closed route that visits every vertex at least once
A shortest route that traverses every edge, ending anywhere

questions.question: In a network, $u$ and $w$ are odd-degree vertices, and every edge of a path from $u$ to $w$ is given a parallel copy. Which vertex degrees change parity?
options: Those of all vertices on the path, which become even
Only those of $u$ and $w$, which both become even
Those of $u$ and $w$, which both stay odd after gaining 2
None, as parallel copies are not counted in the degree

questions.question: For a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, the course construction pairs the odd-degree vertices at minimum total shortest-path distance and duplicates the chosen paths. How is the optimal route length obtained?
options: Total edge length, since duplicates cost nothing
Twice the total edge length, once per direction
Total edge length plus the minimum pairing cost
Total edge length plus all pair distances listed

questions.question: A town's street network falls into two parts with no street between them. Can a Chinese postman route be found for this network?
options: Yes: walk each part with its own closed route.
No: a single closed route cannot reach both parts.
Yes: duplicate paths between odd vertices first.
Only if every vertex in both parts has even degree.

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 3, $B$–$C$ 2, $C$–$D$ 4, $D$–$A$ 5 and $A$–$C$ 7, total 21; A and $C$ are its odd-degree vertices. What is the length of an optimal Chinese postman route?

A network consists of the triangle $A$–$B$–$C$ (lengths 2, 3, 4) and the triangle $A$–$D$–$E$ (lengths 1, 5, 3), sharing vertex $A$; total length 18. What is the length of an optimal Chinese postman route?

In a network, the minimum pairing of odd vertices pairs $P$ with $R$, whose shortest path is $P$–$Q$–$X$–$R$, and $S$ with $T$, joined by the edge $S$–$T$. Which edges does the optimal postman route traverse twice?
options: New edges $P$–$R$ and $S$–$T$
Only $S$–$T$, joining adjacent odd vertices

questions.question: A connected network has six odd-degree vertices. In the Chinese postman construction, how many shortest paths are duplicated?
options: 6, one for each odd vertex
15, one per possible pairing
3, one for each pair of odd vertices
2, as each path fixes three vertices

questions.question: After duplicating the chosen shortest paths, the augmented street network has only even degrees, and an Euler tour of it is found. How is this tour used as the postman's route in the original network?
options: Copies are skipped, so the route covers each street once.
Copies are walked as separate trips from the post office.
Two tours are needed, one for originals and one for copies.
Walking a copy of a street means walking that street again.

questions.question: In the Chinese postman construction, the cost of pairing two odd vertices is their shortest-path distance. Why the shortest-path distance?
options: The pair must be joined by a direct edge, whose length is the cost.
Linking a pair repeats a route between them; the shortest adds least.
The route with the fewest edges is used, so the cost counts edges.
The longest route is used so that every street near the pair is covered.

questions.question: A connected network with total edge length 40 has odd vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ with shortest-path distances $d_{AB}=4$, $d_{CD}=5$, $d_{AC}=3$, $d_{BD}=3$, $d_{AD}=6$, $d_{BC}=6$. What is the length of an optimal Chinese postman route?

Street lengths: $A$–$B$ 6, $A$–$C$ 1, $A$–$E$ 4, $B$–$D$ 1, $C$–$D$ 1, $C$–$E$ 5, $D$–$E$ 3 (sum 21); vertices $A$, $C$, $D$ and $E$ have odd degree. How long is the shortest closed route that covers every street?
A network has the triangle $A$–$B$–$C$ with lengths 2 on $A$–$B$, 3 on $B$–$C$, 4 on $C$–$A$, and the edge $C$–$D$ of length 5. Which closed route is an optimal Chinese postman route?
options: $A$–$B$–$C$–$D$–$A$, of length 14
$A$–$B$–$C$–$D$–$C$–$A$, of length 19

questions.question: In a connected undirected network with nonnegative edge lengths, a proposed closed route covers every edge but walks one edge three times. Why can this route not be shorter than the best route in which no edge is walked more than twice?
options: Removing two of the three traversals keeps parity and coverage.
Three traversals are needed when the edge joins two odd vertices.
Walking an edge three times is fine whenever the edge is short.
It cannot happen, since closed routes walk each edge an even number of times.

questions.question: In a connected undirected network whose edge lengths are all strictly positive, when does the optimal Chinese postman route have length equal to the total edge length?
options: Exactly when every vertex of the network has even degree
Whenever all degrees are even, and sometimes otherwise
Exactly when at most two vertices have odd degree
Whenever the network is connected, whatever the degrees

questions.question: A depot $O$ is joined to three villages $X$, $Y$, $Z$ by roads of lengths 2, 3 and 5, and there are no other roads. A gritting lorry must drive every road and return to $O$. What is the length of an optimal route?

A network of total length 40 has exactly two odd vertices $P$ and $R$, at shortest-path distance 9, so its optimal postman route is 49. A new street $P$–$R$ of length 6 is added. What is the new optimal route length?
options: 46, below the previous 49
55, as the new street adds 6
49, as $P$ and $R$ stay paired
40, the original total length
